cards.q: What is congestion avoidance in QoS and what tool implements it?
cards.a: Congestion avoidance drops packets before a queue overflows to prevent tail-drop and TCP global synchronization. The tool is WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection), which randomly drops lower-priority traffic as the queue fills.

cards.q: What problem does tail drop cause and why is it bad?
cards.a: Tail drop discards the last packets in a full queue, causing TCP global synchronization where TCP windows collapse together, plus burst loss for voice and retransmit efficiency loss.

cards.q: How do the RED/WRED thresholds behave as queue depth grows?
cards.a: Below the min threshold there is no drop, from min to max the random drop rate rises, and above max the queue is full so all packets are dropped.

cards.q: How does WRED weight drops per traffic class?
cards.a: WRED is weighted per class/DSCP: voice (EF) has no drop or the highest min threshold, video (AF) is moderate, and best effort is aggressive, so premium traffic drops last.

cards.q: What command enables WRED and what variants does it support?
cards.a: random-detect enables WRED, random-detect dscp enables per-DSCP weighting, and random-detect precedence enables per-precedence weighting. Min/max thresholds define the drop curve.

cards.q: What is ECN and how does it interact with WRED?
cards.a: ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) marks packets (using ECT/CE bits) instead of dropping them when WRED would drop, so TCP backs off, making it TCP-friendly.
Apply WRED where congestion is real: egress WAN (to protect voice/video), core queues (to avoid TCP sync), and at the edge with drop profiles.

cards.q: ACLs/clients still experience tail drop even though WRED is intended to prevent it; what is the likely cause?
cards.a: WRED is not applied (random-detect not enabled in the policy, or the policy not attached with service-policy output).

cards.q: TCP synchronization persists despite using WRED; what is the likely cause?
cards.a: All classes share the same drop profile, so there is no weighting. Configure differentiated min/max thresholds per class so drops are spread.

cards.q: What does WRED stand for and what makes it different from plain RED?
cards.a: WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection) is RED applied per class/DSCP, so different traffic classes get different drop profiles and premium traffic drops last.

cards.q: What are the three queue thresholds in WRED/RED?
cards.a: min (below = no drop), max (random drop reaches max rate), and full (above max = drop all).

cards.q: When WRED is about to drop, what does ECN do instead and why?
cards.a: ECN marks the packet (ECT/CE bits) instead of dropping it, so TCP backs off without losing the packet, which is TCP-friendly.
